tier_reason: Public harness at benchmarks/ (run-clickbench.sh, scorers/score-clickbench.py, run-oltp-ro.sh, build-pgo.sh) on branch archive/v0.2-main-2026-09-15, with rustc 1.96.0 pinned, -Ctarget-cpu=neoverse-v2 + dist profile (fat LTO) + PGO, and c8g.4xlarge Graviton4 all stated. It scores against a vendored ClickBench ClickHouse c8g.4xlarge row and runs PostgreSQL 18.3 head-to-head for OLTP. That meets A for what the kit documents, but not for the README's 18.5% figure.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'On the ClickBench combined score, pgrust scored 18.5% faster than ClickHouse and hundreds of times faster than PostgreSQL' (pgrcolumnar), and sysbench oltp_read_only 30% higher throughput than PostgreSQL 18.3 at 300 GB. The published benchmark kit does not back the 18.5%. Its README gives only a combined score 'around 0.93 measured (~7% ahead of ClickHouse's published c8g.4xlarge row)': much faster cold, slightly faster hot, worse on load time and data size. Its scorer calls this the formula behind a public '8.6% ahead of ClickHouse' statement. OLTP read-only is 1.25-1.40x vs PostgreSQL 18.3 (PGO build; non-PGO 20-30 points lower), and read-write is near parity (~1.03x).
corrections.baseline: ClickHouse (vendored published ClickBench c8g.4xlarge row dated 2026-07-19, not re-run by the harness); PostgreSQL 18.3 (run head-to-head by the harness for OLTP and ClickBench)
corrections.workload: ClickBench 43 queries on pgrcolumnar (pgrust's built-in columnar layout), c8g.4xlarge with 500 GiB gp2. The official ClickBench protocol is used: cold try 1, hot min(try 2, try 3). Results are scored with pgrust's own pairwise 'combined' formula (hot^0.6 * cold^0.2 * load^0.1 * size^0.1) against a single pinned ClickHouse leaderboard row, not the leaderboard ranking. pgrust is not on the official ClickBench leaderboard. OLTP: sysbench oltp_read_only, 10 tables x 130M rows (~300 GB), and pgbench read-write vs PostgreSQL 18.3 on i8g.xlarge.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.96.0 (pinned in rust-toolchain.toml, LLVM 22). Benchmark builds use -Ctarget-cpu=neoverse-v2, cargo --profile dist (fat LTO) and PGO (-Cprofile-generate / -Cprofile-use via benchmarks/build-pgo.sh). Published binaries are generic and will not reproduce the numbers exactly.
corrections.hardware: AWS c8g.4xlarge (Graviton4 / Neoverse V2, 16 vCPU, 32 GB, 500 GiB gp2 EBS) for ClickBench. OLTP used an i8g.xlarge server with a c8g.2xlarge load client.
corrections.caveats: The README's 18.5%-over-ClickHouse headline conflicts with its own published benchmark kit (~0.93 combined, ~7% ahead; scorer cites '8.6% ahead'). The kit's scorer says the 'combined' number is pgrust's own weighting, not ClickBench's official metric. The ClickHouse side is a pinned 2026-07-19 leaderboard row, not re-run. ClickHouse's current c8g.4xlarge row (2026-09-26) scores about 0.82x the pinned row on pgrust's formula (hot 0.95x, cold 0.72x, load 175 vs 287 s, size 9.5 vs 15.3 GB; derived from page data), so the documented ~7% lead likely does not hold against current ClickHouse. The README's benchmarks/ link 404s on main; the harness survives only on the archive/v0.2-main-2026-09-15 and v0.3-beta branches. The blog's '300x faster analytics' does refer to ClickBench vs PostgreSQL; its SUM() walkthrough (~9.6x over a Volcano baseline) is illustrative. The previously published >50% OLTP gain was revised to 30%, and the Kubernetes vs bare-EC2 discrepancy (50-60%) is unexplained. The review by Greg Smith is an expert review, not an independent third-party suite. Performance is tuned for Graviton4 only (the JIT targets Graviton4). The project describes itself as not production-ready.

notes: The OLTP-vs-PostgreSQL comparison is a genuine head-to-head run by the harness. The ClickHouse win depends on pgrust's own pairwise score against a stale leaderboard row and on a README number the kit does not reproduce. Kept at A for the kit-documented figures, with claimed_speedup corrected. The orchestrator may prefer PostgreSQL as the primary baseline.

tier_reason: ClickBench is a well-known independent third-party suite. Its run scripts are public (ClickHouse/ClickBench firebolt/, with result, subresult and scan caches disabled) and it shows Firebolt beating DuckDB on hot runs across AWS instance types. The engine is a closed Docker binary with no compiler or flags, so it cannot be A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: The '#1 on ClickBench' claim is Firebolt's own launch statement (Show HN and company blog, 2025-06-25: 'instantly took the top spot'); the leaderboard does not show it today. On the current leaderboard (Firebolt rows dated 2026-08-29), all figures derived from page data: vs DuckDB (native), hot-run geomean ratio is 0.64 on c6a.4xlarge (~1.6x faster) and 0.27-0.33 on c6a.metal, c7a.metal-48xl and c8g.metal-48xl (~3-3.8x faster). Cold runs are 1.6-2.3x slower than DuckDB, and Combined is ~10% better on c6a.4xlarge. vs ClickHouse (2026-09-26 rows): hot is roughly parity (0.85-1.04), cold is 1.25-1.8x slower, and ClickHouse leads on Combined on every machine except c6a.large. Approximate Combined rank is ~9th of ~133 entries on c6a.4xlarge and ~6th of ~85 on c8g.4xlarge.
corrections.hardware: ClickBench AWS instances: c6a.large/xlarge/2xlarge/4xlarge/metal (AMD EPYC, 3rd gen), c7a.metal-48xl (AMD EPYC, 4th gen), c8g.4xlarge and c8g.metal-48xl (Graviton4). Single node, 500 GB gp2 per ClickBench convention.
corrections.baseline: DuckDB and ClickHouse via the ClickBench leaderboard (Firebolt wins vs DuckDB on hot runs; roughly ties ClickHouse hot and trails it cold and on Combined)
corrections.caveats: The '#1 on ClickBench' claim is a June 2025 vendor statement; the current leaderboard shows Umbra, CedarDB, Salesforce Hyper and ClickHouse ahead on Combined. Firebolt's wins are hot-run only; its cold-run times are much worse than DuckDB's and ClickHouse's, and its data size is larger than ClickHouse's (15.8 vs ~9.5 GB). ClickBench tags the entry 'ClickHouse derivative' and 'proprietary'. The engine ships as a closed Docker image (ghcr.io/firebolt-db/engine) under Elastic License 2.0 (non-OSI), and the GitHub repo holds only deployment scripts and docs. No compiler or flags are disclosed, so the specific optimizations cannot be inspected.

notes: Real entry with genuine independent-suite evidence, but the record overstated the result as '#1, ahead of ClickHouse, DuckDB and ~100+ engines'. Only the hot-run win over DuckDB is robust on current data. Leaderboard ratios and ranks were computed by replicating the page's own scoring JS over data.generated.js. License confirmed as Elastic License 2.0 from LICENSE.md (API spdx NOASSERTION).
